claim: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by a panoply of social, communicative, and sensory anomalies.
source: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by a panoply of social, communicative, and sensory anomalies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) and a review article (Robertson and Baron-Cohen, 2017), establishing it as accepted knowledge in the field.

claim: Audio-visual integration is intact in ASD and in line with optimal models of cue combination.
source: We show that audio-visual integration is intact in ASD and in line with optimal models of cue combination
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Experiment 1 and Figure 1, showing that ASD subjects combine cues optimally.

claim: Multisensory behavior is anomalous in ASD because this group operates under an internal model favoring integration versus segregation.
source: yet multisensory behavior is anomalous in ASD because this group operates under an internal model favoring integration (vs. segregation).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 and Figure 2, showing that ASD subjects show larger biases and monotonic increases in bias with spatial disparity.

claim: During explicit reports of common cause across spatial or temporal disparities, individuals with ASD were less likely to report common cause, particularly at small cue disparities.
source: Paradoxically, during explicit reports of common cause across spatial or temporal disparities, individuals with ASD were less and not more likely to report common cause, particularly at small cue disparities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiments 3 and 4, shown in Figure 3, demonstrating reduced amplitude of common cause reports in ASD.

claim: Formal model fitting revealed differences in both the prior probability for common cause (p-common) and choice biases between ASD and control groups.
source: Formal model fitting revealed differences in both the prior probability for common cause (p-common) and choice biases
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 4, showing differences in p-common and pcombined parameters.

claim: P-common and choice biases are dissociable in implicit but not explicit causal inference tasks.
source: which are dissociable in implicit but not explicit causal inference tasks.
evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical derivation and modeling framework presented in the Methods section and Figure 4A, showing that pcombined conflates p-common and pchoice in explicit tasks.

claim: There is a presence of an explicit compensatory mechanism in ASD, with these individuals putatively having learned to compensate for their bias to integrate in explicit reports.
source: the presence of an explicit compensatory mechanism in ASD, with these individuals putatively having learned to compensate for their bias to integrate in explicit reports.
evidence: This claim is based on the pattern of results showing increased p-common in implicit tasks but decreased pcombined in explicit tasks, suggesting a compensatory strategy. This is speculative inference from the data.

claim: Individuals with ASD show different internal models in attributing world causes to sensory signals relative to neurotypical individuals given identical sensory cues.
source: this pattern of results suggests (i) different internal models in attributing world causes to sensory signals in ASD relative to neurotypical individuals given identical sensory cues
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing differences in causal inference behavior (Figures 2, 3) and modeling results (Figure 4) between ASD and control groups.

claim: Causal inference is the process of inferring a causal structure linking sensory signals to hidden world causes.
source: Here, we posit causal inference – the process of inferring a causal structure linking sensory signals to hidden world causes – as one such computation.
evidence: This is a definition based on established computational neuroscience literature, specifically citing Körding et al., 2007.

claim: Humans combine sensory signals weighted by their reliability.
source: In fact, an array of studies Ernst and Banks, 2002; Hillis et al., 2002; Alais and Burr, 2004; Kersten et al., 2004 have suggested that humans combine sensory signals weighted by their reliability.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing optimal cue combination in humans.

claim: Humans perform causal inference in solving a wide array of tasks including spatial localization, orientation judgments, oddity detection, rate detection, verticality estimation, spatial constancy, speech perception, time-interval perception, and heading estimation.
source: It is well established that humans perform causal inference in solving a wide array of tasks, such as spatial localization (Körding et al., 2007; Odegaard et al., 2015; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015; Rohe and Noppeney, 2016), orientation judgments (van den Berg et al., 2012), oddity detection (Hospedales and Vijayakumar, 2009), rate detection (Cao et al., 2019), verticality estimation (de Winkel et al., 2018), spatial constancy (Perdreau et al., 2019), speech perception (Magnotti et al., 2013), time-interval perception (Sawai et al., 2012), and heading estimation (Acerbi et al., 2018; Dokka et al., 2019), among others.
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to prior research demonstrating causal inference across multiple domains.

claim: Claims that multisensory perception is anomalous in ASD are abundant and well established.
source: Namely, the claims that multisensory perception is anomalous in ASD are abundant and well established (see Baum et al., 2015 and Wallace et al., 2020, for recent reviews)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two review articles summarizing the literature on multisensory perception in ASD.

claim: Optimal cue combination for visual and vestibular signals is intact in ASD.
source: In this vein, we have demonstrated that optimal cue combination for visual and vestibular signals is intact in ASD (Zaidel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors demonstrating intact visuo-vestibular cue combination in ASD.

claim: The root of the multisensory deficits in ASD may not be in the integration process itself, but in establishing an internal model suggesting when signals ought to be integrated vs. segregated.
source: In turn, the root of the multisensory deficits in ASD may not be in the integration process itself (see Noel et al., 2020, for recent evidence suggesting intact integration over a protracted timescale in ASD), but in establishing an internal model suggesting when signals ought to be integrated vs. segregated – a process of causal inference.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior research (Zaidel et al., 2015; Noel et al., 2020) and the hypothesis being tested in the current manuscript.

claim: 31 individuals with ASD (mean age 15.2±0.4 years; 5 females) and 34 age-matched neurotypical controls (16.1±0.4 years; 9 females) participated in Experiment 1.
source: individuals with ASD (n=31; mean ± S.E.M; 15.2±0.4 years; 5 females) and age-matched neurotypical controls (n=34, 16.1±0.4 years; 9 females)
evidence: This is a direct report of the participant demographics for Experiment 1.

claim: Subjects with ASD localized the visual stimulus as well as neurotypical subjects (ASD: 6.83±0.68°; control: 6.30±0.49°).
source: Overall, subjects with ASD (6.83±0.68°) localized the visual stimulus as well as neurotypical subjects (6.30±0.49°, Figure 1D, no group effect, F[1, 57]=0.88, p=0.35, η2=0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1, with statistical analysis showing no significant difference between groups.

claim: Visual discrimination thresholds decreased as visual reliability decreased (high reliability: 1.10±0.07°, medium: 4.76±0.36°, low: 13.96±0.82°).
source: As visual reliability decreased (lighter colors), the psychometric curves became flatter indicating larger spatial discrimination thresholds (high reliability: 1.10±0.07°, medium: 4.76±0.36°, low: 13.96±0.82°).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1, showing the effect of visual reliability manipulation on thresholds.

claim: The effect of visual reliability on thresholds was equal across both ASD and control subject groups.
source: This effect of visual reliability was equal across both subject groups (group × reliability interaction, F[2, 114]=0.11, p=0.89, η2<0.01), with visual thresholds being equal in control and ASD across all reliability levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data showing no interaction between group and reliability.

claim: Auditory threshold estimation was not possible for 6 of the 31 subjects within the ASD group due to a lack of modulation in their reports as a function of cue location.
source: Auditory threshold estimation was not possible for 6 of the 31 subjects within the ASD group (Figure 1D, green, R2 value <0.50), due to a lack of modulation in their reports as a function of cue location
evidence: This is a direct report of data quality issues for a subset of ASD participants in Experiment 1.

claim: Auditory thresholds were similar across neurotypical controls and the ASD cohort where threshold estimation was possible.
source: Auditory thresholds were similar across neurotypical controls and the ASD cohort where threshold estimation was possible (t57=–1.14, p=0.21, Cohen's d=0.11).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference in auditory thresholds between groups.

claim: Both control and ASD subjects combined cues in line with predictions from statistical optimality (control, slope = 0.93, 95% CI = [0.85–1.04]; ASD, slope = 0.94, 95% CI = [0.88–1.08]).
source: Figure 1E demonstrates that indeed both control (gradients of black) and ASD (gradients of red) subjects combined cues in line with predictions from statistical optimality (control, slope = 0.93, 95% CI = [0.85–1.04]; ASD, slope = 0.94, 95% CI = [0.88–1.08]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing measured and predicted audio-visual thresholds according to optimal integration theory.

claim: Statistically optimal integration of multisensory cues is intact in ASD across sensory pairings (audio-visual and visuo-vestibular).
source: These results generalize previous findings from Zaidel et al., 2015 and suggest that across sensory pairings (e.g. audio-visual here, visuo-vestibular in Zaidel et al., 2015) statistically optimal integration of multisensory cues is intact in ASD.
evidence: This claim is based on the current experimental data combined with prior research (Zaidel et al., 2015).

claim: Measured and predicted visual weights according to optimal cue combination were well matched in control (slope = 0.97, 95% CI = [0.92–1.02]) and ASD (slope = 0.99, 95% CI = [0.93–1.05]) groups.
source: Importantly, measured and predicted visual weights according to optimal cue combination were well matched in control (Figure 1H, black, slope = 0.97, 95% CI = [0.92–1.02]) and ASD (Figure 1H, red, slope = 0.99, 95% CI = [0.93–1.05]) groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing measured and predicted visual weights in the forced fusion task.

claim: Measured visual weights were not different between ASD and control groups at any reliability level.
source: Measured visual weights were also not different between groups at any reliability (F[2, 114]=1.11, p=0.33, η2=0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference in visual weights between groups.

claim: ASD subjects dynamically reweighted auditory and visual cues on a trial-by-trial basis depending on their relative reliabilities.
source: Thus, just as their neurotypical counterparts, ASD subjects dynamically reweighted auditory and visual cues on a trial-by-trial basis depending on their relative reliabilities.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data showing that visual weights varied with reliability in ASD subjects, similar to controls.

claim: Individuals with ASD did not show impairments in integrating perceptually congruent and near-congruent auditory and visual stimuli.
source: Together, this pattern of results suggests that individuals with ASD did not show impairments in integrating perceptually congruent (and near-congruent) auditory and visual stimuli.
evidence: This claim is a summary inference from the experimental data in Experiment 1 showing intact optimal cue combination in ASD.

claim: 21 individuals with ASD (17.32±0.57 years; 5 females) and 15 age-matched neurotypical controls (16.86±0.55 years; 7 females) participated in Experiment 2.
source: Individuals with ASD (n=21, 17.32±0.57 years; 5 females) and age-matched neurotypical controls (n=15, 16.86±0.55 years; 7 females, see Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2 for overlap in cohorts across experiments)
evidence: This is a direct report of the participant demographics for Experiment 2.

claim: Individuals with ASD showed a larger bias in auditory localization than the control group (F[1, 34]=5.44, p=0.025, η2=0.13).
source: Overall, individuals with ASD showed a larger bias (i.e. absolute value of the mean of the cumulative Gaussian fit) in auditory localization than the control group (see Figure 2A and B, respectively, for control and ASD cohorts; F[1, 34]=5.44, p=0.025, η2=0.13).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 with statistical analysis showing a significant group difference.

claim: How the bias varied with spatial disparity significantly differed between ASD and control groups (group × disparity interaction: F[7, 168]=3.50, p=0.002, η2=0.12).
source: Further, how the bias varied with spatial disparity (∆) significantly differed between the groups (group × disparity interaction: F[7, 168]=3.50, p=0.002, η2=0.12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data showing a significant interaction effect.

claim: While the bias saturated at higher spatial disparities in neurotypical subjects, the bias increased monotonically as spatial disparity increased in the ASD group.
source: While the bias saturated at higher ∆ in neurotypical subjects, as expected under causal inference, the bias increased monotonically as ∆ increased in the ASD group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2, shown in Figure 2A and B, demonstrating different patterns of bias as a function of disparity.

claim: Despite increasing spatial discrepancy, ASD subjects tended to integrate the cues, as if they nearly always utilized visual signals to localize the auditory cue and did not readily switch to a worldview where the auditory and visual cues did not come from the same world source.
source: Thus, despite increasing spatial discrepancy, ASD subjects tended to integrate the cues, as if they nearly always utilized visual signals to localize the auditory cue and did not readily switch to a worldview where the auditory and visual cues did not come from the same world source.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data showing monotonic increase in bias with disparity in ASD subjects.

claim: The effect of visual cue reliability was similar in both ASD and control groups (group × reliability interaction, F[2, 168]=1.05, p=0.35, η2=0.01).
source: The effect of visual cue reliability was similar in both groups (group × reliability interaction, F[2, 168]=1.05, p=0.35, η2=0.01)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant interaction between group and reliability.

claim: The ASD group had a larger linear coefficient in the regression model relating auditory bias to spatial disparity across all visual reliabilities (ANOVA: F[1, 34]=6.69, p=0.014, η2=0.16).
source: As shown in Figure 2C, across all visual reliabilities, the ASD group had a larger linear coefficient (a1, ANOVA: F[1, 34]=6.69, p=0.014, η2=0.16), again indicating a monotonic increase in bias with cue spatial disparity.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of regression coefficients from the experimental data.

claim: The linear term accounted for more variance in the ASD data than controls (ANOVA: F[1, 34]=7.08, p=0.012, η2=0.17).
source: Results showed that not only the linear term accounted for more variance in the ASD data than controls (Figure 2D and x-axis, ANOVA: F[1, 34]=7.08, p=0.012, η2=0.17)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing the variance explained by linear regression models.

claim: The addition of a cubic term significantly improved fits in the control, but not ASD, group (ANOVA: F[1, 34]=9.87, p=0.003, η2=0.22).
source: but also the addition of a cubic term significantly improved fits in the control, but not ASD, group (Figure 2D and y-axis, partial R2, ANOVA: F[1, 34]=9.87, p=0.003, η2=0.22).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing the improvement in model fit from adding a cubic term.

claim: ASD subjects were not able to down-weight the impact of visual cues on auditory localization at large spatial disparities, resulting in larger errors in auditory localization.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that contrary to predictions from causal inference – where disparate cues should affect one another at small but not large disparities, i.e., only when they may reasonably index the same source – ASD subjects were not able to down-weight the impact of visual cues on auditory localization at large spatial disparities, resulting in larger errors in auditory localization.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data showing continued integration at large disparities in ASD subjects.

claim: Psychometric thresholds, bias, and goodness of fit were not significantly different between the ASD and control cohorts in unisensory localization tasks across visual and auditory modalities and across all reliabilities (all p>0.09 for thresholds, all p>0.11 for bias, all p>0.26 for R-squared).
source: Psychometric thresholds (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, all p>0.09), bias (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, all p>0.11), and goodness of fit (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, all p>0.26) were not significantly different between the ASD and control cohorts, across visual and auditory modalities, and across all reliabilities.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of unisensory localization data showing no significant differences between groups.

claim: The same effect of anomalous implicit causal inference was replicated in a visual heading discrimination task requiring the attribution of optic flow signals to self-motion and/or object-motion.
source: Last, to further bolster the conclusion that individuals with ASD show anomalous implicit causal inference, we replicate the same effect in a very different experimental setup.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 5 (visual heading discrimination task) presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: While heading biases are present during intermediate self-velocity disparities and object-velocity disparities for controls and ASD subjects, they disappear during large cue discrepancies in control subjects, but not ASD subjects.
source: Importantly, however, the results demonstrate that while heading biases are present during intermediate self-velocity disparities and object-velocity disparities for controls and ASD subjects (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D), they disappear during large cue discrepancies in control subjects, but not ASD subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the visual heading discrimination task shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The process of integrating information across modalities is normal in ASD once a correct internal model of the causal structure of the world has been formed.
source: Together, these results suggest that in ASD the process of integrating information across modalities is normal (see Zaidel et al., 2015) once a correct internal model of the causal structure of the world has been formed.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing intact optimal cue combination but anomalous causal inference in ASD.

claim: The process of inferring causal structure is anomalous in ASD.
source: However, the process of inferring this causal structure – the set of relations between hidden sources and sensory signals that may have given rise to the observed data – is anomalous.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing anomalous behavior in causal inference tasks in ASD.

claim: Individuals with ASD seem to operate under the assumption that sensory cues ought to be integrated most of the time, even for large disparities.
source: Namely, individuals with ASD seem to operate under the assumption that sensory cues ought to be integrated most of the time, even for large disparities.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data showing continued integration at large disparities in ASD subjects.

claim: 23 individuals with ASD (16.14±0.51 years; 5 females) and 24 age-matched neurotypical controls (17.10±0.42 years; 7 females) participated in Experiment 3.
source: Individuals with ASD (n=23; 16.14±0.51 years; 5 females) and age-matched neurotypical controls (n=24; 17.10±0.42 years; 7 females; see Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2 for overlap in cohorts with previous experiments)
evidence: This is a direct report of the participant demographics for Experiment 3.

claim: Most subjects reported a common source more frequently at smaller rather than larger spatial disparities (F[8, 259]=94.86, p<0.001, η2=0.74).
source: As expected, most subjects reported a common source more frequently at smaller rather than larger ∆ (Figure 3 F[8, 259]=94.86, p<0.001, η2=0.74).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 with statistical analysis showing a significant effect of disparity.

claim: Eight of the individuals with ASD (approximately one-third of the cohort) did not modulate their explicit common cause reports as a function of spatial disparity, despite good auditory and visual localization.
source: Interestingly, while this pattern was true for all individual control subjects, eight of the individuals with ASD (i.e. ~⅓ of the cohort) did not modulate their explicit common cause reports as a function of spatial disparity, despite good auditory and visual localization (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of data quality issues for a subset of ASD participants in Experiment 3.

claim: Both ASD and control groups reported common cause less frequently for lower visual reliability (F[2, 74]=10.68, p<0.001, η2=0.22).
source: For lower visual reliability (Figure 3, from A-C), both groups reported common cause less frequently (F[2, 74]=10.68, p<0.001, η2=0.22).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 with statistical analysis showing a significant effect of reliability.

claim: There was a decreased likelihood of reporting common cause, across spatial disparities and visual cue reliabilities, in ASD relative to controls (F[1, 37]=11.6, p=0.002, η2=0.23).
source: A striking difference between experimental groups was the decreased likelihood of reporting common cause, across spatial disparities and visual cue reliabilities, in ASD relative to controls (Figure 3A–C shades of black vs. shades of red, F[1, 37]=11.6, p=0.002, η2=0.23).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 with statistical analysis showing a significant group difference.

claim: The pattern of results using an explicit causal inference task is opposite from that described for the implicit task of auditory localization, where individuals with ASD were more, and not less, likely to combine cues.
source: This pattern of results using an explicit causal inference task is opposite from that described for the implicit task of auditory localization, where individuals with ASD were more, and not less, likely to combine cues.
evidence: This claim is a comparison of results across Experiments 2 and 3, highlighting the paradoxical pattern of behavior.

claim: Both control and ASD participants perceived a common source most frequently at a spatial disparity close to 0°, and there was no group difference for this parameter (control = 0.30±1.33°; ASD = 0.48±1.9°; F[1, 37]<0.01, p=0.92, η2<0.01).
source: Both control and ASD participants perceived a common source most frequently at a ∆ close to 0°, and there was no group difference for this parameter (control = 0.30±1.33°; ASD = 0.48±1.9°; F[1, 37]<0.01, p=0.92, η2<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of Gaussian fits to the explicit common cause reports, showing no difference in the mean parameter.

claim: The peak amplitude of the best-fit Gaussian was smaller for the ASD than the control group (control = 0.75±0.02; ASD = 0.62±0.05; F[1, 37]=8.44, p=0.0006, η2=0.18).
source: The peak amplitude of the best-fit Gaussian was smaller for the ASD than the control group (control = 0.75±0.02; ASD = 0.62±0.05; F[1, 37]=8.44, p=0.0006, η2=0.18)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of Gaussian fit parameters showing a significant group difference in amplitude.

claim: The width of the Gaussian fit was smaller in the ASD compared to the control group (control = 30.21±2.10°; ASD = 22.35±3.14°; F[1, 37]=7.00, p=0.012, η2=0.15).
source: The width of the Gaussian fit was smaller in the ASD compared to the control group (control = 30.21±2.10°; ASD = 22.35±3.14°; F[1, 37]=7.00, p=0.012, η2=0.15)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of Gaussian fit parameters showing a significant group difference in width.

claim: The range of spatial disparities at which ASD participants perceived a common source was significantly smaller than in controls.
source: suggesting that the range of spatial disparities at which ASD participants perceived a common source was significantly smaller than in controls.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the Gaussian width parameter difference between groups.

claim: 21 individuals with ASD (15.94±0.56 years; 5 females) and 13 age-matched neurotypical controls (16.3±0.47 years; 5 females) participated in Experiment 4.
source: Twenty-one individuals with ASD (15.94±0.56 years; 5 females) and 13 age-matched neurotypical controls (16.3±0.47 years; 5 females, see Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is a direct report of the participant demographics for Experiment 4.

claim: The ASD group had smaller amplitudes in synchrony reports at small temporal disparities (ASD = 0.83±0.04; control = 0.98±0.01; t-test: t32=7.75, p<0.001, Cohen's d>2).
source: Just as for spatial disparities, the ASD group had smaller amplitudes (ASD = 0.83±0.04; control = 0.98±0.01; Figure 3D; t-test: t32=7.75, p<0.001, Cohen's d>2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4 with statistical analysis showing a significant group difference.

claim: At small temporal disparities, individuals with ASD perceived the stimuli as originating from a common cause less frequently than control subjects did.
source: suggesting that at small ∆ individuals with ASD perceived the stimuli as originating from a common cause less frequently than control subjects did.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the amplitude difference in synchrony reports between groups.

claim: The ASD group exhibited larger Gaussian widths in synchrony reports (control = 171.68±13.17; ASD = 363±55.63 ms; t-test: t32=2.61, p=0.01, Cohen's d=0.9).
source: Further, the ASD group exhibited larger Gaussian widths (control = 171.68±13.17; ASD = 363±55.63 ms; t-test: t32=2.61, p=0.01, Cohen's d=0.9)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4 with statistical analysis showing a significant group difference.

claim: The larger Gaussian widths in ASD reflect more frequent reports of common cause at large temporal disparities.
source: reflecting more frequent reports of common cause at large temporal disparities.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the Gaussian width parameter difference between groups.

claim: The finding of larger temporal binding windows in ASD than control corroborates a multitude of reports (see Feldman et al., 2018 for a meta-analysis of 53 studies).
source: This second effect corroborates a multitude of reports demonstrating larger 'temporal binding windows' in ASD than control (see Feldman et al., 2018 for a meta-analysis of 53 studies).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current experimental data and a citation to a meta-analysis of prior research.

claim: Explicit reports of common cause across spatial and temporal disparities agree in suggesting a lower likelihood of inferring a common cause at small temporal disparities in ASD relative to neurotypical controls.
source: Overall, therefore, explicit reports of common cause across spatial and temporal disparities agree in suggesting a lower likelihood of inferring a common cause at small temporal disparities - including no disparity - in ASD relative to neurotypical controls (see e.g. Noel et al., 2018b; Noel et al., 2018a, for previous reports showing altered overall tendency to report common cause during temporal disparities in ASD, although these reports typically focus on the size of 'binding windows').
evidence: This claim is a summary of results from Experiments 3 and 4, with citations to prior research showing similar effects.

claim: Correlational analyses between psychometric features and symptomatology measures (AQ and SCQ) demonstrated weak to no association.
source: Correlational analyses between psychometric features distinguishing control and ASD individuals (i.e. linear and cubic terms accounting for auditory biases during large audio-visual spatial disparities, amplitude and width of explicit common cause reports during spatial and temporal disparities) and symptomatology measures, i.e., autism quotient (AQ; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001) and social communication questionnaire (SCQ; Rutter et al., 2003) demonstrated weak to no association.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analyses of the experimental data with symptomatology measures.

claim: The only significant correlation surviving Bonferroni-correction was between the width of the Gaussian function describing synchrony judgments as a function of temporal disparity and SCQ scores (Type II regression: r=0.52, p=0.002).
source: Of the 12 correlations attempted ([AQ + SCQ] × [amplitude + width] × [temporal + spatial] + [AQ + SCQ] × [linear + cubic terms]), the only significant relation (surviving Bonferroni-correction) was that between the width of the Gaussian function describing synchrony judgments as a function of temporal disparity and SCQ scores (Type II regression: r=0.52, p=0.002; see Smith et al., 2017 for a similar observation).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis of the experimental data with symptomatology measures.

claim: Allowing only for a difference in the choice parameters (lapse rate, bias, and pchoice) between the control and ASD cohorts could only partially account for observed differences between these groups in the implicit task (EVE=0.91).
source: In the implicit task (Figure 4B, top panel), allowing only for a difference in the choice parameters (lapse rate, bias, and pchoice; magenta) between the control and ASD cohorts, could only partially account for observed differences between these groups (explainable variance explained, EVE=0.91, see Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results comparing different model variants.

claim: Differences between the control and ASD data in the implicit task could be better explained if the prior probability of combining cues, pcommon, was also significantly higher for ASD relative to control observers (p=4.5 × 10–7, EVE=0.97, ∆AIC = 1 × 103).
source: Instead, differences between the control and ASD data could be better explained if the prior probability of combining cues, pcommon, was also significantly higher for ASD relative to control observers (Figure 4D, p=4.5 × 10–7, EVE=0.97, ∆AIC between model varying only choice parameters vs. choice and inference parameters = 1 × 103).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing better fit when pcommon is allowed to vary.

claim: For the explicit task, different lapse rates and biases between ASD and controls could not explain their differing reports (EVE = 0.17).
source: For the explicit task, different lapse rates and biases between ASD and controls could also not explain their differing reports (as for the implicit task; EVE = 0.17).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing poor fit when only lapse parameters vary.

claim: In the explicit task, it is not possible to dissociate the prior probability of combination (pcommon) and choice biases.
source: Differently from the implicit task, however, we cannot dissociate the prior probability of combination (i.e. pcommon) and choice biases, given that the report is on common cause (Figure 4A, see Methods and Supplementary file 4 for additional detail).
evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical derivation of the causal inference model for explicit tasks.

claim: Allowing for a lower pcombined in ASD could better explain the observed differences between ASD and control explicit reports (EVE = 0.69, ∆AIC = 1.3 × 103).
source: Allowing for a lower pcombined in ASD could better explain the observed differences between ASD and control explicit reports (Figure 4C; EVE = 0.69, ∆AIC relative to a model solely varying lapse rate and bias = 1.3 × 103).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing better fit when pcombined is allowed to vary.

claim: The aggregate ASD subject had a higher pcommon than the aggregate control observer in the implicit task (p=1.8 × 10–4).
source: This is illustrated for the ASD aggregate subject relative to the aggregate control subject in Figure 4D (p=1.8 × 10–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results comparing parameter estimates between groups.

claim: The differing pattern of results in the implicit and explicit tasks can be ascribed to differences in the choice bias, which may reflect a compensatory strategy by ASD observers.
source: Under the assumption that an observer's expectation for cues to come from the same cause (pcommon) is formed over a long timescale, and hence is the same across the implicit and explicit tasks, we can ascribe the differing pattern of results in the tasks (i.e. increased pcommon in ASD in the implicit task, yet a decreased pcombined in the explicit task) to differences in the choice bias (i.e. the added component from pcommon to pcombined). This bias may in fact reflect a compensatory strategy by ASD observers since we found their pcommon (uncorrupted by explicit choice biases) to be roughly three times as large as that of the aggregate control observer (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the modeling results, involving speculation about the nature of the compensatory mechanism.

claim: The causal inference model provided a good and comparable fit for both ASD and control subjects, with the model explaining more than 80% of explainable variance in all but one subject.
source: The causal inference model provided a good and comparable fit for both ASD and control subjects (Figure 4E) with the model explaining more than 80% of explainable variance in all but one subject (Figure 4E, blue dot).
evidence: This claim is supported by the goodness-of-fit analysis of the causal inference model applied to individual subject data.

claim: In agreement with the aggregate data, individuals with ASD had a higher prior probability of common cause than control subjects during the implicit task (p=0.02).
source: Nonetheless, in agreement with the aggregate data, individuals with ASD had a higher prior probability of common cause than control subjects (Figure 4F) during the implicit task (p=0.02), where pcommon can be estimated independently from pchoice.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of individual subject parameter estimates from the causal inference model.

claim: When estimating pcombined for the explicit task, the parameter estimates extracted from the individual fits suggested no difference between ASD and control subjects (p=0.26).
source: When estimating pcombined (i.e. the combination of pcommon and pchoice) for the explicit task (Figure 4G), the parameter estimates extracted from the individual fits suggested no difference between ASD and control subjects (p=0.26)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of individual subject parameter estimates from the causal inference model.

claim: The aggregate and single subject fits concord in suggesting an explicit compensatory mechanism in individuals with ASD.
source: Importantly, the aggregate and single subject fits concord in suggesting an explicit compensatory mechanism in individuals with ASD, given that pcommon is higher in ASD than control (when this parameter can be estimated in isolation) and a measure corrupted by explicit choice biases (i.e. pcombined) is not.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the modeling results from both aggregate and individual subject analyses.

claim: Individual subjects' pcommon and pcombined as estimated by the model did not correlate with ASD symptomatology, as measured by the AQ and SCQ (all p>0.17).
source: Individual subjects' pcommon and pcombined as estimated by the model did not correlate with ASD symptomatology, as measured by the AQ and SCQ (all p>0.17).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analyses of model parameters with symptomatology measures.

claim: For the implicit task, alternative A (forced fusion) is a considerably better model than alternative B (forced segregation), but still worse than the model in the main text.
source: For the implicit task, two main observations must be noted. First, all models perform worse than that presented in the main text (y-axis is difference to the model presented in the main text, with higher Akaike Information Criterion [AIC] indicating a worse quality of fit). Second, Alternative A is substantially better than Alternative B, but still worse than the model in the main text.
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison using AIC, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: ASD subjects do perform causal inference and not pure forced fusion, yet they overweight integration versus segregation compared to their neurotypical counterparts.
source: Thus, seemingly individuals with autism spectrum disorder do perform causal inference and not pure forced fusion, yet they overweight integration (vs. segregation) compared to their neurotypical counterparts.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the model comparison results showing that forced fusion is better than forced segregation but worse than the causal inference model.

claim: Across domains (visuo-vestibular and audio-visual), optimal cue combination is intact in ASD.
source: These observations generalize a previous report (Zaidel et al., 2015) and suggest that across domains (visuo-vestibular in Zaidel et al., 2015 audio-visual here), optimal cue combination is intact in ASD.
evidence: This claim is based on the current experimental data combined with prior research (Zaidel et al., 2015).

claim: The well-established anomalies in multisensory behavior in ASD may not be due to a dysfunctional process of multisensory integration per se, but one of impaired causal inference.
source: This suggests that the well-established anomalies in multisensory behavior in ASD - e.g., biases (see Baum et al., 2015 and Wallace et al., 2020, for reviews) – may not be due to a dysfunctional process of multisensory integration per se, but one of impair causal inference.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results, drawing on prior literature about multisensory anomalies in ASD.

claim: The juxtaposition between an impaired ability for causal inference yet the presence of an intact ability for optimal cue combination may suggest a deficit in a specific kind of computation and point toward anomalies in particular kinds of neural motifs.
source: The juxtaposition between an impaired ability for causal inference yet the presence of an intact ability for optimal cue combination may suggest a deficit in a specific kind of computation and point toward anomalies in particular kinds of neural motifs.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference about the neural basis of the observed behavioral differences.

claim: An additional algorithmic component in causal inference relative to optimal cue combination models is the presence of non-linear operations such as marginalization.
source: Indeed, an additional algorithmic component in causal inference (Körding et al., 2007) relative to optimal cue combination models (Ernst and Banks, 2002) is the presence of non-linear operations such as marginalization.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the computational differences between causal inference and optimal cue combination models.

claim: Marginalization corresponds to 'summing out' nuisance variables, allows for non-linearities, and may be neurally implemented via divisive normalization.
source: This operation corresponds to 'summing out' nuisance variables, allows for non-linearities, and may be neurally implemented via divisive normalization (see Beck et al., 2011 for detail on marginalization and the relationship between this operation and divisive normalization).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about marginalization and its neural implementation, citing Beck et al., 2011.

claim: Not all proposed neural network models of causal inference rely on divisive normalization.
source: In fact, while not all proposed neural network models of causal inference rely on divisive normalization (see Cuppini et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019 for networks performing causal inference without explicit marginalization), many do (e.g. Yamashita et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to prior research on neural network models of causal inference.

claim: Divisive normalization is a canonical neural motif thought to operate throughout the brain, wherein neural activity from a given unit is normalized by the joint output of a normalization neural pool.
source: Divisive normalization is a canonical neural motif (Carandini and Heeger, 2011), i.e., thought to operate throughout the brain, wherein neural activity from a given unit is normalized by the joint output of a normalization neural pool.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about divisive normalization, citing Carandini and Heeger, 2011.

claim: The broad anomalies observed in ASD may be underpinned by an alteration in a canonical computation (causal inference), which in turn is dependent on a canonical neural motif (divisive normalization).
source: Thus, the broad anomalies observed in ASD may be underpinned by an alteration in a canonical computation, i.e., causal inference, which in turn is dependent on a canonical neural motif, i.e., divisive normalization.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference linking the behavioral findings to neural mechanisms.

claim: Rosenberg et al., 2015 suggested that anomalies in divisive normalization can account for a host of perceptual anomalies in ASD, such as altered local vs. global processing, altered visuo-spatial suppression, and increased tunnel vision.
source: Rosenberg et al., 2015, suggested that anomalies in divisive normalization – specifically a reduction in the amount of inhibition that occurs through divisive normalization – —can account for a host of perceptual anomalies in ASD, such as altered local vs. global processing (Happé and Frith, 2006), altered visuo-spatial suppression (Foss-Feig et al., 2013), and increased tunnel vision (Robertson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to prior research linking divisive normalization to perceptual anomalies in ASD.

claim: The suggestion from altered divisive normalization, to altered marginalization, and in turn altered causal inference and multisensory behavior is well aligned with known physiology in ASD and ASD animal models showing decreased GABAergic signaling.
source: This suggestion – from altered divisive normalization, to altered marginalization, and in turn altered causal inference and multisensory behavior – is well aligned with known physiology in ASD and ASD animal models showing decrease GABAergic signaling (Lee et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is speculative inference linking the computational findings to known physiology in ASD, citing relevant research.

claim: The suggestion is well aligned with the comorbidity between ASD and seizure activity.
source: the comorbidity between ASD and seizure activity (Jeste and Tuchman, 2015)
evidence: This claim is based on a citation to prior research on the comorbidity between ASD and seizures.

claim: The suggestion is well aligned with the hypothesis that ASD is rooted in an increased excitation-to-inhibition ratio (E/I imbalance).
source: and the hypothesis that ASD is rooted in an increased excitation-to-inhibition ratio (i.e. E/I imbalance; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on a citation to prior research proposing the E/I imbalance hypothesis of ASD.

claim: Individuals with ASD show a reduced tendency to explicitly report common cause during small cue disparities, across both spatial and temporal disparities.
source: A second major empirical finding is that individuals with ASD seem to explicitly report common cause less frequently than neurotypical controls. Here we demonstrate a reduced tendency to explicitly report common cause during small cue disparities, across both spatial and temporal disparities
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiments 3 and 4.

claim: A reduced tendency to explicitly report common cause during small temporal disparities has previously been observed in ASD.
source: This has previously been observed within the temporal domain (Noel et al., 2018b; Noel et al., 2018a)
evidence: This claim is based on citations to prior research by the authors.

claim: Multisensory simultaneity judgments are frequently normalized to peak at '1', obfuscating the effect of reduced tendency to report common cause at small disparities.
source: yet frequently multisensory simultaneity judgments are normalized to peak at '1' (e.g. Woynaroski et al., 2013; Dunham et al., 2020), obfuscating this effect.
evidence: This claim is based on citations to prior research and methodological critique.

claim: The reduced tendency to overtly report common cause across spatial and temporal domains in ASD is indicative of a choice bias that may have emerged as a compensatory mechanism to their increased implicit tendency to bind information across sensory modalities.
source: More importantly, the reduced tendency to overtly report common cause across spatial and temporal domains in ASD (even when implicitly they seem to integrate more, and not less often) is indicative of a choice bias that may have emerged as a compensatory mechanism to their increased implicit tendency to bind information across sensory modalities.
evidence: This claim is speculative interpretation of the pattern of results across implicit and explicit tasks.

claim: The presence of a putative compensatory mechanism is important to note, particularly when a significant fraction of the characterization of (multi)sensory processing in ASD relies on explicit tasks.
source: The presence of this putative compensatory mechanism is important to note, particularly when a significant fraction of the characterization of (multi)sensory processing in ASD relies on explicit tasks.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the implications of the findings for the broader literature on sensory processing in ASD.

claim: This finding highlights the importance in characterizing both implicit and explicit perceptual mechanisms, particularly when framed under a strong theoretical foundation and using model-based analyses.
source: Further, this finding, highlights the importance in characterizing both implicit and explicit perceptual mechanisms – particularly when framed under a strong theoretical foundation (Ernst and Banks, 2002; Körding et al., 2007) and using model-based analyses (e.g. Lawson et al., 2017; Lieder et al., 2019) – given that explicit reports may not faithfully reflect subjects' percepts.
evidence: This claim is an inference about methodological implications, citing relevant theoretical and methodological papers.

claim: The finding that individuals with ASD do not change their worldview from integration to segregation even at large sensory disparities may result in sensory anomalies and reflect the slow updating of expectations.
source: The finding that individuals with ASD do not change their worldview (i.e. from integration to segregation, even at large sensory disparities) may result in sensory anomalies and reflect the slow updating of expectations (Vishne et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is speculative interpretation of the findings, citing relevant research on expectation updating in ASD.

claim: Anomalies in causal inference may have the potential of explaining seemingly disparate phenotypes in ASD – anomalous perception and repetitive behaviors.
source: Thus, anomalies in causal inference may have the potential of explaining seemingly disparate phenotypes in ASD – anomalous perception and repetitive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference about the broader implications of the findings for understanding ASD phenotypes.

claim: Stereotypy could result from attempting to align incoming sensory evidence with the (inflexible) expectations of what that sensory input ought to be.
source: Stereotypy could result from attempting to align incoming sensory evidence with the (inflexible) expectations of what that sensory input ought to be.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference about the relationship between causal inference anomalies and stereotypy in ASD.

claim: By leveraging a computational framework and systematically measuring perception at each step, we can ascribe anomalies in multisensory behavior to the process of inferring the causal structure linking sensory observations to their hidden causes.
source: In conclusion, by leveraging a computational framework (optimal cue combination and causal inference; Ernst and Banks, 2002; Körding et al., 2007) and systematically measuring perception at each step (i.e. unisensory, forced cue integration, and causal inference) across a range of audio-visual multisensory behaviors, we can ascribe anomalies in multisensory behavior to the process of inferring the causal structure linking sensory observations to their hidden causes.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main conclusion, based on the experimental data and computational modeling.

claim: The anomaly in causal inference results in perceptual biases, but these biases are driven by a canonical computation that has gone awry.
source: Of course, this anomaly results in perceptual biases (see the current results and Baum et al., 2015 for an extensive review), but the point is that these biases are driven by a canonical computation that has gone awry.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the findings, emphasizing the computational nature of the deficit.

claim: Given the known E/I imbalance in ASD and the fact that causal inference may require marginalization but optimal cue combination does not, we can speculatively suggest a bridge from neural instantiation to behavioral computation.
source: Further, given the known E/I imbalance in ASD (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Lee et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020) and the fact that causal inference may require marginalization but optimal cue combination does not (Beck et al., 2011), we can speculatively suggest a bridge from neural instantiation to behavioral computation
evidence: This claim is speculative inference linking neural mechanisms to computational processes and behavior.

claim: E/I imbalance may disrupt divisive normalization (neural implementation), which leads to improper marginalization (algorithm) and thus altered causal inference (computation) and multisensory perception (biases in behavior) in ASD.
source: E/I imbalance may disrupt divisive normalization (neural implementation), which leads to improper marginalization (algorithm) and thus altered causal inference (computation) and multisensory perception (biases in behavior) in ASD.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference proposing a mechanistic chain from neural to behavioral levels.

claim: A total of 91 adolescents (16.25±0.4 years; 20 females) took part in a series of up to five behavioral experiments.
source: A total of 91 adolescents (16.25±0.4 years; 20 females) took part (completely or partially) in a series of up to five behavioral experiments
evidence: This is a direct report of the overall participant demographics across all experiments.

claim: 48 participants were neurotypical controls (16.5±0.4 years; 13 females).
source: Forty-eight of these were neurotypical controls. Individuals in the control group (16.5±0.4 years; 13 females)
evidence: This is a direct report of the control group demographics.

claim: 43 participants were diagnosed as within ASD (16.0±0.5 years; 7 females).
source: The other 43 participants (16.0±0.5 years; 7 females) were diagnosed as within ASD.
evidence: This is a direct report of the ASD group demographics.

claim: All participants were screened at enrollment with SCQ and/or the AQ to afford a measure of current ASD symptomatology and rule out concerns for ASD in control subjects.
source: All participants were screened at enrollment with SCQ (Rutter et al., 2003) and/or the AQ (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001) to afford (1) a measure of current ASD symptomatology and (2) rule out concerns for ASD in control subjects.
evidence: This is a direct report of the screening procedures used in the study.

claim: There was no individual with ASD below the recommended SCQ cutoff.
source: There was no individual with ASD below the recommended SCQ cutoff
evidence: This is a direct report of the screening results for the ASD group.

claim: Only 2 out of 47 control subjects were above the SCQ cutoff.
source: and only 2 (out of 47) control subjects above this cutoff (Surén et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a direct report of the screening results for the control group.

claim: There was almost no overlap in ASD and control AQ scores.
source: Similarly, there was almost no overlap in ASD and control AQ scores (with only 3 out of 47 control individuals having a higher AQ score than the lowest of the individuals with ASD).
evidence: This is a direct report of the screening results comparing AQ scores between groups.

claim: All individuals with ASD were above the AQ cutoffs recommended by Woodbury-Smith et al., 2005 and Lepage et al., 2009 (cutoff scores of 22 and 26), but not by Baron-Cohen et al., 2001 (cutoff score of 36).
source: All individuals with ASD were above the AQ cutoffs recommended by Woodbury-Smith et al., 2005 and Lepage et al., 2009 (respectively, cutoff scores of 22 and 26), but not by Baron-Cohen et al., 2001 (cutoff score of 36).
evidence: This is a direct report of the screening results for the ASD group relative to different published cutoffs.

claim: Inclusion in the ASD group required that subjects have a confirmed diagnosis of ASD according to the DSM-5 by a research-reliable clinical practitioner and no history of seizure or other neurological disorders.
source: Inclusion in the ASD group required that subjects have (1) a confirmed diagnosis of ASD according to the DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) by part of a research-reliable clinical practitioner and (2) no history of seizure or other neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a direct report of the inclusion criteria for the ASD group.

claim: A subset of the individuals with ASD were assessed by the ADOS-2, and no difference was observed in the AQ, SCQ, or psychometric estimates between individuals with ASD with and without the ADOS assessment (all p>0.21).
source: A subset of the individuals with ASD were assessed by the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2, Lord et al., 2012), and no difference was observed in the AQ, SCQ, or psychometric estimates between individuals with ASD with and without the ADOS assessment (all p>0.21).
evidence: This is a direct report of additional assessment procedures and their results.

claim: The intelligence quotient (IQ) as estimated by the WAIS was available for a subset of the ASD participants (n=10, or 22% of the cohort), whose average score was 103±9 (S.E.M.), this being no different from the general population (which by definition has a mean of 100).
source: Similarly, the intelligence quotient (IQ) as estimated by the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) was available for a subset of the ASD participants (n=10, or 22% of the cohort), whose average score was 103±9 (S.E.M.), this being no different from the general population (which by definition has a mean of 100).
evidence: This is a direct report of IQ assessment results for a subset of ASD participants.

claim: All subjects had normal visual and auditory acuity, as characterized by parents' and/or participants' reports.
source: All subjects had normal visual and auditory acuity, as characterized by parents' and/or participants' reports.
evidence: This is a direct report of the sensory acuity screening procedure.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the Baylor College of Medicine (protocol number H-29411) and written consent/assent was obtained.
source: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the Baylor College of Medicine (protocol number H-29411) and written consent/assent was obtained.
evidence: This is a direct report of the ethical approval and consent procedures.
